big: In March 2026 the Nifty 50 fell 11.3% and industry assets under management slid 10.1% in one month. Yet investors put ₹40,450 crore into equity funds that month, per AMFI. Your job is to make sure your clients are among those who stayed.

lines: The papers say markets are crashing, but Meena has not called. Should I leave her alone?
No. Silence in a fall is rarely calm. Call before she calls you, and bring her own plan, not a market forecast.

h: What a SIP does in a fall
alt: Six monthly instalments of 10,000 rupees buying units while the price slides 11.3 percent and then recovers

At ₹88.7 the same ₹10,000 bought 112.7 units, against 100 units at ₹100.
Same money, about 13% more units, because the price was 11.3% lower.
The price recovers, and the cheaper units come along for the ride.
₹60,000 bought 634 units, at an average cost of ₹94.6.

alt: A shield with what a good call does and what it must not do
caps: Call before they call you, with context and their own plan in hand.
A good call restates the plan and shows what the SIP bought at lower prices.
Never call the bottom, and never promise a date for the recovery.
title: On the phone, after a fall
stops: Remind them what the plan assumed
Show what the SIP bought at low prices
Say this is the bottom, so buy more
Promise a recovery by a fixed date

intro: What investors did in the month the Nifty 50 fell 11.3% to 22,331.
note: Part of the AUM fall was net outflows from debt funds, so the index move is the fairer market figure to quote.

q: A fund's price falls 20%, from ₹100 to ₹80. How many more units does a client's fixed SIP instalment buy at ₹80 than at ₹100?
why: The price fell 20%, but units move as the reciprocal: 1 divided by 0.8 is 1.25, so the gain in units is larger than 20%.
A fixed sum divided by a lower price always gives more units. The same number would need the price to stay unchanged.
₹10,000 buys 100 units at ₹100 and 125 units at ₹80. That is 25% more for the same money.
Units do not rise by half the fall. The link is reciprocal, so a 20% fall lifts units by 25%, not about 12%.

q: A colleague tells clients markets fell 10.1% in March 2026, quoting the fall in industry AUM from AMFI. What is the weakness in that statement?
opts: AUM mixes market moves with flows; the Nifty 50's 11.3% is fairer
AUM never falls within a month, so the figure must be an error
Nothing, since industry AUM is the official measure of market return
AMFI reports AUM only for equity funds, so it cannot be used
why: AUM moves with market prices and with money in or out. Debt funds saw large net outflows that month, so the index is cleaner.
AUM can fall in a month, and it did. The 10.1% is a real AMFI figure, so the issue is its meaning, not an error.
AUM is not a return measure. It changes with flows as well as prices, so it should not be passed off as a market return.
AMFI reports AUM for all fund types, debt included. That is partly why the 10.1% is not a pure equity-market figure.

q: The Nifty is down 11% this month. A client in her third year of SIP has not called you. What do you do?
opts: Wait for her to call, since contact may unsettle her
Call, restate her plan, and show what the SIP bought
Email a market outlook that predicts a recovery date
Offer to pause her SIP until the market settles
why: Waiting leaves her alone with the headlines. Clients who hear from you first tend to ask before they act.
It gives context and a plan, not a forecast. Showing the cheaper units her SIP bought turns the fall into something useful.
No one can predict a date, and a wrong forecast costs trust. Context and her own plan are worth more than an outlook.
A pause skips the instalments that buy at low prices. Offering it first teaches her that the plan is to be dropped in a fall.

q: A client who needs ₹15 lakh for a flat in 18 months wants to sell his equity fund after a 25% fall. What is the most honest approach?
opts: Tell him to hold everything, since every fall recovers in time
Agree to sell everything, because any fall means the plan failed
Wait 18 months, then sell whatever the fund is worth by then
Split by goal, since the flat money needs a safer home
why: No one can promise a recovery before his date. Money due in 18 months cannot wait for one, which is the real problem.
A fall is not proof the plan failed. Selling long-term money at the low makes a paper loss real, so only what is due soon should move.
That makes the flat depend on the market's mood in 18 months. It repeats the original mistake of holding near-term money in equity.
Hand-holding does not mean never selling. Near-term money belongs in safer funds, while long-term money can stay with the plan.

pts: Falls of 10% or more happen in most years, so a plan should assume them. A SIP buys more units when prices are lower.
Call before they call you: restate the plan, and never predict the bottom or promise a recovery date.
Selling at the low and waiting to feel safe usually means buying back higher. Money needed soon never belonged in equity.
